name: Hurricane Isaias
headline: The first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 peaked at Category 3 over the Gulf, then hit near Destin, Florida, on 9 October as a Category 2 with 105 mph winds.
numbers: 118 mph at Jay, 116 mph at Oriole Beach (NWS Mobile, preliminary)
About 730,000 early on 10 Oct (AP, poweroutage.com); some reports up to about 900,000
4 (AP, 10 Oct), 6 (AccuWeather, 14 Oct), 9 (WUSF, 11 Oct): tallies differ; NWS Mobile, preliminary: 1 direct and 2 indirect in its area
timeline: Tropical Depression Nine forms in the southern Gulf (Bay of Campeche) on 6 Oct (best track); NWS lists a disturbance there from 4 Oct.
Becomes Tropical Storm Isaias in the morning; rapid intensification 7–8 Oct (Climate Central).
Becomes the season's first hurricane: late 7 Oct local time per The Weather Channel, 8 Oct per NASA. Eight named storms had formed before it.
Reaches Category 3, the season's first major hurricane; rising wind shear then disrupts its structure.
Landfall near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 with sustained winds of 105 mph.
Weakens over Alabama and becomes post-tropical; remnants spread heavy rain into the Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic; tornadoes in Georgia and the Carolinas.
Night-time satellite imagery shows widespread darkness around Pensacola and US 98 on 11 Oct; by 14 Oct lighting looks similar to pre-storm conditions (NASA).
Moody's RMS estimates insured losses at $2.5–4.5 billion, best estimate $3.5 billion.

sections.In brief: Hurricane Isaias was the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026. It strengthened to Category 3 over the Gulf before making landfall near Destin, Florida, on 9 October as a Category 2 hurricane with sustained winds of 105 mph. Its main impacts were destructive winds, power outages, storm surge and inland flooding across the Southeast.
Why it intensified so fast: Isaias met exceptionally warm Gulf water, a moist atmosphere and a window when wind shear was not strong enough to disrupt its core. Its winds rose by 40 mph in the 24 hours ending early on 8 October, above the rapid-intensification threshold of about 35 mph in 24 hours (Yale Climate Connections).

Warm water supplied energy: sea-surface temperatures along its path were about 30–31 °C (86–88 °F), unusually warm for October. Warm water feeds a hurricane heat and moisture, helping its thunderstorms strengthen and its winds accelerate.
Moist air supported the thunderstorms: Isaias initially kept drier air approaching from the west out of its inner core, so its central thunderstorms stayed organized.

Wind shear (the change in wind speed or direction with height) stayed manageable for a while: Isaias strengthened despite moderate shear of roughly 15–20 kt. It did not need completely calm upper-level winds.
In short, the storm had abundant ocean energy and enough atmospheric protection to turn that energy into stronger winds. Warm water alone would not have guaranteed rapid intensification.
sections.Why the strengthening stopped: As Isaias approached the northern Gulf Coast, stronger upper-level winds raised the shear (to about 27–39 kt) while dry air wrapped toward its circulation. These conditions disrupted the storm and weakened it from Category 3 to Category 2 before landfall. The warm water could fuel it but could not offset the atmospheric disruption. It still produced destructive gusts and widespread tree damage.
Where the damage was worst: The Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama had major wind damage: fallen trees, damaged roofs and downed power lines. The strongest gusts were west of the centre: NWS Mobile's preliminary report lists 118 mph at Jay, 116 mph at Oriole Beach and 114 mph at Whiting Field (the report notes that the stations probably did not sample the peak); NASA, citing preliminary National Weather Service observations, reported 102 mph at Pensacola City Hall.

Coastal flooding: the Panama City Beach Pier gauge recorded a peak water level of 5.59 ft above Mean Higher High Water, roughly the normal high-tide line (NWS Tallahassee, preliminary). This is a gauge reading, not the flood depth at every nearby property.

Heavy rain: Bellwood, Alabama, recorded 12.97 inches in about 13 hours; parts of western North Carolina received up to 9 inches (The Weather Channel). Where a stalled front added to the hurricane's rain, many sites reported 10–20 inches in total (WUSF).

Power outages: counts depend on the time and the tracker. AP, using poweroutage.com, reported more than 726,000 customers without power early on 10 Oct and 396,000 on 11 Oct; The Weather Channel, citing poweroutage.us, put the peak at about 900,000 and AccuWeather at about 930,000.
Tornadoes: the system spawned tornadoes in Georgia and the Carolinas, including near Newington, Georgia, west of Allendale, South Carolina, and near Candor, North Carolina.

Deaths: tallies differ by source and date: at least 4 (AP, 10 Oct), at least 6 (AccuWeather, 14 Oct) and 9 (WUSF, 11 Oct, including six reported by Florida's governor). NWS Mobile's preliminary report counts one direct and two indirect deaths in its area; NWS Tallahassee lists none in its area.
Why it was notable: A very late first hurricane: although Isaias was the ninth named storm, it did not become the season's first hurricane until 7–8 October. AccuWeather says that broke a 121-year record for the latest first hurricane of an Atlantic season. The quiet season is consistent with El Niño's wind shear over the Atlantic (see The setup), but a quiet season did not prevent one damaging storm.
It strengthened quickly, then weakened before landfall: unusually warm Gulf water drove rapid intensification, and strong shear trimmed its sustained winds before landfall.
sections.Did climate change contribute?: Climate Central's rapid analysis estimated that the water Isaias rapidly intensified over was 1.4 °C (2.4 °F) warmer on average than it would have been without human-caused climate change, and that such temperatures were made 4 to 600 times more likely. Its preliminary storm estimate is about 7 mph more wind and no change in category. This supports a contribution from climate change to the storm's ocean-energy supply, not a claim that climate change alone caused the hurricane or its rapid intensification. Moisture, wind shear and the storm's internal organization also mattered.
Recovery and estimated costs: As of 17 October the focus is recovery, not an approaching storm. NASA's Black Marble night-lights imagery (VIIRS on NOAA-20) showed widespread darkness around Pensacola and the US 98 corridor on 11 October; by 14 October, lighting patterns looked similar to pre-storm conditions. NASA cautions that these images complement, rather than replace, ground-level outage reports.

On 16 October, Moody's RMS estimated industry insured losses at $2.5–4.5 billion, with a best estimate of $3.5 billion. Wind accounts for most of it; storm surge, inland flooding and NFIP losses together are only about $250 million. Other modelers are lower: KCC about $3 billion, Cotality $2–3 billion and Verisk $1–2 billion. These are preliminary insured-loss estimates, not a final tally of economic damage or uninsured losses.
sections.The setup: El Niño shear suppresses the Atlantic (17% of normal energy); the Gulf is the exception.
sections.The trigger: Low over the southern Gulf ~7 Oct, MJO phases 1–2 favourable.
sections.What amplified it: Gulf water 28–29.5 °C; shear ~20 kt. Capped by rising shear (27–39 kt) and dry air before landfall as Cat 2.
sections.Still open: Figures are preliminary. NHC's final Tropical Cyclone Report will confirm peak intensity, landfall details and the official death toll.
